title: The palace in flames (Genesis Rabbah 39:1)
hook: Abraham sees a burning palace and asks if it has no owner; the owner looks out
tomorrow: Jacob lay down on stones. he woke up with one. how?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Noah's cedars. They could have asked, and almost nobody did. Today, someone who does ask, out loud, and gets an answer.

Night, on a long road. A traveler comes over a rise and sees a great building, a palace, lit up from inside. Or burning. He stops. Nobody runs out with buckets. Nobody runs in. And he asks out loud, to no one at all: is it possible this palace has no one in charge of it?
screen: `NIGHT, ON A LONG ROAD.` → `A PALACE, LIT UP. OR BURNING.` → `IS NO ONE IN CHARGE?`

segments.voice: Genesis Rabbah tells this parable about Abraham, just before God says to him, "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house." In the parable, the master of the palace looks out at the traveler and says: I am the master of this palace. So with Abraham, the midrash says. He kept asking: is it possible the world has no one guiding it? And the Holy One looked out at him and said: I am the Master of the world. Here's the twist. The Hebrew phrase, birah doleket, can be heard as a palace full of light or a palace in flames, and readers take it both ways. Lit up: Abraham sees the world's order and beauty and asks who built it. In flames: Abraham sees a world full of cruelty and fire and asks how its owner can let it burn. Either way, Abraham doesn't pretend the palace is fine. He asks out loud. And the owner doesn't scold him for asking. He looks out, and answers: I'm here, it's mine. Then, right after, the call: get thee out. In this story the one who asks who's in charge is the one who gets sent.
screen: `A PALACE, AND NO ONE AROUND.` · `I AM THE MASTER OF THIS PALACE.` · `LIT UP, OR ON FIRE?` · `THE ASKER IS SENT.` · then, large: `THE PALACE HAS AN OWNER.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound around you that means someone is looking after something: a fridge humming, a furnace, traffic lights, a neighbor's footsteps. Stay with that one sound for the sit. Let it carry the traveler's question: who keeps this going?
The palace in flames: Abraham's parable in Genesis Rabbah. A shining or burning palace, a question out loud, and the owner looking out.
Your line: the palace has an owner. And the owner answers the one who asks. That's day fifteen seventy-six.
